newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Hungary says Slovak dam founded on self-interest.
newsitem.headline: Hungary says Slovak dam founded on self-interest.

text.p: Hungary accused neighbouring Slovakia on Monday of selfishly pursuing its own interests without regard for the environment or Hungary when it diverted the Danube's waters for a hydroelectric project in 1992.

Foreign Ministry lawyer Gyorgy Szenasi told the International Court of Justice the project was an illegal act of self-enrichment which was wreaking havoc on the environment and depriving Hungarians of vital water resources.
"These acts were a serious violation of the territorial sovereignty of Hungary," he told the United Nations court.
Szenasi was speaking on the first day of court hearings on a long-running dispute over the Gabcikovo dam project which has led to strained relations between Budapest and Bratislava.
The Slovak dam was originally part of a 1977 plan agreed by the then Communist governments of Czechoslovakia and Hungary.
But Hungary suspended work on a companion dam downstream at Nagymaros in 1989 following pressure from environmental groups, and in 1992 it pulled out of the project altogether.
Slovakia pressed ahead with the $500 million hydroelectric scheme at Gabcikovo after its split from Czechoslovakia in 1993 but it agreed to submit the dispute to the U.N. court.

It says Hungary broke its part of the agreement and should therefore pay damages to Slovakia, arguing that Budapest made the environmental problems worse by halting construction of the Nagymaros dam which would have offset the effects of Gabcikovo.
Hungary says it abandoned the project because of concerns about its effect on water supplies and the environment.
Reduced water flow and falling ground water levels, it says, have had a devastating effect on the flora and fauna of the Danube's flood plains as well as on agriculture and fisheries.
The Worldwide Fund for Nature (WWF) said at the end of 1995 that the scheme was threatening up to 90 percent of the marshy region's rich plant and wildlife.
Szenasi said some areas affected by the project had lost 90 percent of their water supply as a result of the Slovak dam.
He said Slovakia had violated international law by unilaterally diverting a river which formed part of its border with Hungary and should be ordered to pay damages.
"These waters are currently being used to generate electricity in Slovakia and it is quite clear to us that this illegal self-enrichment must be compensated," he said.
Hungary will spend most of this week presenting detailed legal arguments and scientific evidence to the court. Slovakia will present its case from March 24 to 27.

Peter Tomka, head of the Slovak delegation, told Reuters he was confident the court would ultimately rule in his country's favour as there had been no legal basis for Hungary's unilateral termination of its 1977 treaty with Slovakia.
He rejected the assertion that Slovakia had blindly followed its own self-interest, saying his country badly needed the power which the hydroelectric scheme was providing.
"This project provides 10 percent of Slovakia's electricity needs. That's a very substantial portion," he said.
The International Court of Justice is the main judicial organ of the United Nations and settles disputes between states in accordance with international law.
The court's 15 judges will visit the dam and view its alleged effects on the Hungarian side of the river in early April. They are expected to deliver their ruling in the autumn.
